effect_mechanism: Trees change farm costs in both directions, mostly through labour. Some systems save cost: In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and cut as mulch required 30 man-days ha−1 less than current farmer management, because it cut the labour needed for weeding [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. In Colombia, production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under silvopastoral systems than under traditional ranching, an estimate from a Bank-commissioned business case attributed to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower animal death and disease [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. Others add cost: in the forest zone of Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping raised labour from 75 to 104 (38%) person-days per hectare per year and variable costs by 34% averaged over the trial, for hedgerow planting, pruning and mulching [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]; and at Ibadan, Nigeria, maize mulched with cut-and-carry tree leaves needed more labour than fertilised or untreated plots, with 96% of the labour going to collecting and managing the mulch and only 4% to weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. A Nigerian alley-cropping model adds two further labour-cost readings, both increases: annual labour for maize production under 4 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping is reported increased by 53 percent against the traditional bush-fallow control, because of the added labour for hedgerow pruning, and under the closer 2 m spacing the model assumes total labour increases by 87 percent, since more hedgerows need pruning [ev_project_cost_ehui90_5, ev_project_cost_ehui90_6].
conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is where the trees' labour falls. Where the trees grow in the field and suppress weeds, as the Rwandan Tephrosia did, weeding labour falls [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]; where tree biomass must be pruned, cut and carried, the extra handling outweighs the weeding saved, and in Nigeria the mulch was grown on a separate plot and carried in [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. Between them sit no-change findings: A cocoa meta-analysis found the higher total production of agroforestry systems is not reflected in the costs compared with monoculture [ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies in low- and middle-income countries reports agroforestry production cost -1.39% against a control across 10 studies, not significant (0.952), with an interval spanning a cost fall and a cost rise (-29.06 to 68.32), pooling agroforestry applied alone or in bundles [ev_project_cost_steward23wp_1]. The Cameroon costs mix establishment and recurrent pruning labour, and its trees were pruned only from the second year [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Colombian figure is a modelled recurrent saving from an upper-middle-income country and does not pool with the relative changes [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. The coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3, ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. The field evidence is otherwise from low-income Rwanda and lower-middle-income Cameroon and Nigeria, within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1, ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. Both readings add to the cost-increase side of this row rather than the cost-saving side: like the Cameroon and Nigeria mulching evidence already here, the extra labour is pruning and handling tree biomass, not time saved on weeding. The 4 m figure is drawn from an earlier cited labour study rather than measured by the modelling authors themselves, and the 2 m figure is the modelling authors' own assumption (more hedgerows to prune at closer spacing), not a measurement. Both are lower-middle-income Nigerian evidence, within the LIC/LMIC target.
